explanations: luna: Abraham asks for this city to be made secure and its people supplied with fruits, a concrete parallel to the section's city fed from hunger and protected from fear. | terra: Abraham asks that the city be secure and that its believing people be provided with fruits, a prayer that joins city, safety, and food like the section’s famine meeting.

luna: The passage names fear, hunger, and loss of wealth as trials and gives glad tidings to the patient, connecting the section's famine-day passage with sabr under hardship. | terra: Fear, hunger, and loss of wealth are named as trials, followed by the command to give good news to the patient; this gathers famine, diminished property, and saving patience in one test.

luna: The section quotes the same root ṣ-b-r in the astonished phrase “فَمَآ أَصْبَرَهُمْ عَلَى ٱلنَّارِ”: endurance here is a doomed daring to face fire, divided from the self-restraint needed on the ascent. | terra: The sarcastic فَمَا أَصْبَرَهُمْ عَلَى النَّارِ makes “patience” an audacity toward Fire, precisely the section’s reversal of the patience that restrains a climber on the pass.
luna: This account of righteousness joins freeing a neck, giving wealth to orphan and poor, and patience in adversity; it gathers the section's passage acts into one moral scene.
luna: In the fasting passage, feeding a poor person appears as a provision when one cannot fast; it concretely joins bodily hunger and feeding the needy, though in a different legal setting.

luna: The answer about what to spend names parents, near kin, orphans, needy people, and travelers, directly collecting the section's relational beneficiaries into a giving scene. | terra: The answer about spending names relatives, orphans, needy people, and the traveler together, concretely joining wealth with the orphan’s kinship and the poor mouth.

luna: The ayah says that if people mix their affairs with orphans, they are their brothers; this makes explicit the kin-like bond behind the section's orphan and same-womb compassion. | terra: Reform is declared best for orphans, and mixing with them is allowed because they are “your brothers,” directly joining the orphan to kinlike belonging.

luna: The ayah warns not to use oaths as a barrier to righteousness, piety, or making peace; it makes the section's oath-and-passage meeting explicit. | terra: Believers are forbidden to make their oaths by God an obstacle to goodness, piety, and reconciliation, directly clarifying how an oath should open toward good action rather than bar it.

luna: The seed multiplied into many ears is a concrete counter-image to the section's expenditure that leaves no gain, showing charity's yield rather than its erasure. | terra: Spending wealth is likened to a grain that grows seven ears, joining generosity to multiplication through plant growth; it supports the section’s final picture of merciful givers becoming a joined growth.
luna: Those who spend without following their gift with reminders or injury receive a reward; this neighboring passage supplies the ethical opposite of the section's showy spending.
luna: A kind word and pardon are better than charity followed by injury, sharpening the section's contrast between public display and actual mercy.

luna: The section's riya (showing-off) meets spending made for people to see: the smooth rock's dust is washed away by rain, and the spenders cannot command anything of what they earned. Its “cannot measure/control” link is the same root q-d-r as 90:5. | terra: The ostentatious spender seeks رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ, then rain strips soil from rock and leaves the spenders unable—لَا يَقْدِرُونَ—to retain any gain; this is the section’s meeting of watched wealth, earth, and failed power.

luna: Against 2:264's showy gift washed off bare stone, this neighboring spend is likened to a garden on high ground whose rain yields fruit; it shows giving that remains fruitful. | terra: Against the bare rock of 2:264, sincere spending is a garden بِرَبْوَةٍ on high ground whose rain doubles its yield; height, rain, earth, and spending now produce lasting fruit.
terra: Whatever people spend or vow is known by God, bringing expenditure, vow, and divine awareness into a single answer to spending for human eyes.
luna: Secret charity is better, though open charity is also good; this directly answers the section's spend-for-people-to-see image.
luna: Those who spend by night and day, privately and publicly, receive reward and fear no grief; it gives a specific faithful counterpart to ostentatious spending.
luna: The ayah says righteousness is not reached until one spends what one loves, making expenditure a threshold to goodness like the section's passage.
luna: The people become brothers after God joins their hearts; this supplies a specific image for the section's compassion binding people together.
luna: Their spending is likened to a freezing wind striking a crop and destroying it; this parallels the section's rain washing away the dust of a showy gift.
terra: What people withhold from God’s bounty سَيُطَوَّقُونَ around their necks on Judgment Day, turning unspent wealth into the very neck-bond that generosity should undo.

luna: The section's mutual compassion “as if from the same womb” meets the ayah's one-soul origin and its explicit “وَٱلْأَرْحَامَ” (wombs), grounding kinship in shared origin. | terra: Human beings spread from one soul and its mate, and the verse invokes الْأَرْحَامَ together with God’s watchfulness, grounding the section’s “as from one womb” account of mutual mercy.
terra: When relatives, orphans, and needy people attend an estate division, the heirs must provide for them from it and speak kindly, making inherited wealth answer kinship and hunger.

luna: Those who consume orphan property unjustly are promised fire in their bellies and a blaze, joining the section's orphan, wealth, and fiery consequence in one warning. | terra: Those who consume an orphan’s property unjustly are only consuming fire into their bellies and will enter a blaze, making stolen orphan-wealth itself become the fire opposite feeding the orphan.

luna: This command lists parents, kin, orphan, needy, neighbor, traveler, and those in bondage as recipients of good treatment, closely matching the section's web of care and release. | terra: The command to do good names relatives, orphans, needy people, travelers, and those under one’s authority together, another concrete social field in which kinship and release from need meet.

luna: The section's root and wording for riya (showing-off) recur in spending wealth to be seen by people, a direct lexical parallel to the false display in 2:264. | terra: Those who spend their wealth رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ enact the exact contradiction developed in the section: human eyes are courted while faith in God and the Last Day is absent.

luna: The expiation for accidental killing includes freeing a believing neck, a separate legal setting that repeats the section's concrete act of releasing a neck. | terra: The accidental-killing ruling repeatedly requires تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ, a direct Quranic occurrence of freeing a neck, though its legal occasion differs from the section’s hunger and oath scenes.
terra: The wrongdoers are granted no guiding road except طَرِيقَ جَهَنَّمَ, turning guidance and path into arrival at the fire rather than escape from it.

luna: The oath-expiration here joins feeding ten poor people with freeing a neck, the very two acts the section says the Quran places together when an oath is expiated. | terra: The expiation for bound oaths joins إِطْعَامُ عَشَرَةِ مَسَاكِينَ with تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ, putting the section’s oath, feeding, needy people, and opened neck in one ruling.
terra: For the one God lets stray, the chest becomes constricted as though climbing into the sky, making ascent the felt image of misguidance rather than release.

luna: This command joins protecting orphan wealth, giving full measure, speaking justly even about kin, and fulfilling a covenant; it gathers the section's orphan, measure, relation, and oath motifs in one ayah. | terra: The command to protect the orphan’s property is immediately joined to giving full measure and weight with justice, bringing orphaned vulnerability, wealth, and exact measuring together.
terra: The man is given God’s signs but slips out of them; 7:176 then explains that those very signs could have raised him before he clung to the earth.

luna: The section explicitly recalls the man who could have been raised by signs but “أَخْلَدَ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ”; this is its clearest image of sticking to the low ground instead of rising by the passage. | terra: The man could have been raised by the signs but أَخْلَدَ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ; 7:175 identifies those signs, so ascent and clinging to earth face one another exactly as in the section.
terra: The departing army goes out boastfully and to be seen by people while barring God’s way, bringing ostentatious human sight and obstruction of the road into the same act.

luna: Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend in God's way face painful punishment, directly tying withheld wealth to the section's refusal and fire. | terra: Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God’s way are promised punishment; 9:35 turns the hoard into heated metal against their bodies.

luna: The hoarded metal is heated in the Fire and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs, giving a bodily fire consequence to the section's wealth-and-fire conjunction. | terra: Hoarded treasure is heated in Hell and used to brand its owners, making unspent wealth meet bodily fire in one concrete reversal.
terra: اثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ and preference for the nearer life enact the downward attachment that the section places opposite being raised by the signs.
terra: Obligatory alms are assigned both to the poor and needy and فِي الرِّقَابِ, making spent wealth serve the section’s feeding and neck-release together.
luna: Believing men and women are each other's allies and mutually uphold good; this parallels the section's repeated mutual urging of patience and mercy.
luna: Joseph's interpretation of seven harsh years consuming what was stored gives a concrete extended famine alongside the section's day of hunger.
luna: The next year of relief, rain, and pressing produce completes the famine sequence with a specific return of provision after scarcity.
terra: Joseph’s brothers come and enter his presence during the famine, supplying the actual arrival prompted by scarcity whose distress and request for measured charity are voiced in 12:88.
terra: A family driven to the city by distress arrives with poor goods and asks Joseph to give full measure and charity, joining famine migration, measured provision, and merciful giving.
terra: Those who deny recreation have fetters on their necks and are companions of the Fire, placing the bound neck, rejection, and fiery side together in one ayah.
terra: Those who remain patient for God, establish prayer, and spend from their provision secretly and openly join patience to rightly directed expenditure rather than display.

luna: Abraham settles descendants by the Sacred House in a barren valley and asks for provision; it joins the section's city, lineage, and need for food in one scene. | terra: Abraham places his offspring in an uncultivated valley at the Sacred House and asks for hearts to incline to them and fruits to provide for them, joining city origins, kin, and food under scarcity.

luna: The command not to undo oaths after confirming them meets the section's image of oaths knotted and then expiated through release and feeding. | terra: The command not to break oaths بَعْدَ تَوْكِيدِهَا treats the sworn bond as something made firm, supplying the binding side of the section’s oath-and-release image.

luna: The spun thread undone after being firm gives a specific reversal for the section's bound-and-released sequence of oath and neck. | terra: The woman who untwists firmly spun yarn becomes the likeness for making oaths deceptive, giving the oath’s undoing a physical unbinding image after 16:91.
terra: Using oaths deceptively makes a firmly planted foot slip, so the oath and the traveler’s footing meet in one warning about losing the way.

luna: The example of a secure, provisioned city made to taste hunger and fear reverses the city that the section says is fed from hunger and secured from fear. | terra: A secure, tranquil town with abundant provision denies God’s favors and is made to taste hunger and fear, reversing the city fed from hunger and secured from fear.
terra: Each person’s record is fastened to his neck, yet on the Last Day it comes out as a book he finds spread open, joining a bound neck to an opening in one judgment scene.
luna: The command to lower the wing of humility out of mercy to one's parents gives an exact downward motion for the section's claim that ascent comes by stooping in compassion.
luna: The command to give the near relative, needy person, and traveler their due makes the section's kinship and feeding acts concrete duties.
luna: The hand is pictured chained to the neck for miserliness and then overextended in spending; this meets the section's neck-release image and the boast of having spent much wealth.
luna: The command not to approach an orphan's property except rightly, followed by fulfilling covenants, joins the section's vulnerable orphan with its oath-bound moral responsibility.
luna: Hearing, sight, and heart are each accountable, connecting the section's gifted faculties and the illusion of being unseen to judgment for their use.
luna: The arrogant walker cannot split the earth or reach the mountains in height; this boundary reverses the section's ascent, which is achieved by bending toward those on the ground.

luna: The day each community is called with its record, those given the record in their right hands, gives the section's right-side company a judgment-scene counterpart to the left-hand record in 69:25.

luna: The section names the root wāw-ṣād-dāl in 90:20; here the cave dog's “بِٱلْوَصِيدِ” (at the threshold) meets sleepers turned to the right and left in one scene. | terra: The sleepers are turned right and left while their dog stretches its forelegs بِالْوَصِيدِ, joining the two sides to the threshold word related to the section’s closing root.
luna: The cave companions send one with their silver into the city to obtain food; this next step after 18:18 connects the threshold scene with the section's city and feeding images.
terra: The garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and a stronger company; 18:42–43 later show the property destroyed and all protective power gone.
terra: Entering his garden while wronging himself, the owner claims it will never perish, supplying the confidence in durable wealth that the later ruin overturns.
terra: When the garden’s fruit is destroyed, its owner turns his hands over what he spent while its trellises collapse, a concrete scene of trusted expenditure becoming loss.
terra: After his garden falls, no company can help him besides God and he cannot defend himself, answering the boast that no one can overpower the wealthy man.
terra: Worldly life is like rain-grown vegetation that becomes dry fragments scattered by wind, while God remains capable over all things; 18:46 identifies wealth and children as its adornment.

terra: Wealth and children are the adornment of the nearer life, while enduring righteous deeds are better and more hopeful, distinguishing what vanishes from what remains after the plant parable of 18:45.

luna: Moses sees fire while traveling and hopes to find “عَلَى ٱلنَّارِ هُدًۭى”; the section contrasts that guiding fire with the fire sealed over the way's end. | terra: Moses sees the fire by the mountain and hopes to find هُدًى at it, uniting the raised waymark and guidance that the section contrasts with the journey ending in a sealed fire.
luna: Moses answers Pharaoh that the Lord gave each thing its form and then guided it, another explicit creation-and-guidance formulation behind the section's sequence.
terra: Whoever takes Satan as ally is led astray and “guided” to the punishment of the Blaze, turning guidance itself toward fire in the same reversal as the section’s failed waymark.
luna: Those whose scales are heavy are successful; this makes measure determine an outcome like the section's division into right and left companies.
luna: Those whose scales are light lose themselves and remain in Hell, completing the contrary measured outcome with a fire destination.

terra: People of means are told not to swear that they will withhold gifts from relatives, needy people, and emigrants; this directly joins an oath, wealth, kinship, and relief of need in the direction the section gives its opening oath.
luna: On the Day of Witness, tongues and hands testify to what people did; this makes the section's given tongue and its hidden actions publicly answerable.
terra: Masters are told to contract emancipation for those seeking it and give them مِن مَّالِ اللَّهِ, joining release from bondage to the transfer of wealth.
luna: The Creator is said to have created everything and determined it with exact measure, another direct creation-and-measure formulation behind the section's sequence.
luna: The faithful neither spend extravagantly nor withhold but keep a middle course, a specific counterpoint to the boast of lavish spending without mercy.

luna: Moses again sees fire during travel and hopes for news or a brand from it; this repeated wayfarer's fire helps mark the reversal to a fire no longer serving as a sign. | terra: Moses sees a fire and goes to it for news or a burning brand, repeating the night traveler’s use of distant fire for orientation and benefit, though this telling does not call the fire itself guidance.
luna: As a neighbor to Moses' fire in 27:7, the scene turns the travel-fire into a blessed divine encounter, completing the image of a fire that guides.

luna: In another telling of Moses' journey, “ءَانَسْتُ نَارًۭا” begins a search for news or a burning brand, a traveling fire opposite the sealed destination-fire. | terra: At the side of the Mount Moses sees a fire and seeks news or a brand for his family, again joining elevation, travel, and visible fire without the explicit هُدًى wording of 20:10.
luna: The neighboring continuation of 28:29 places the call at the blessed tree on the valley's right side; the fire-lit journey opens into guidance rather than enclosure.
terra: The secure sanctuary to which fruits are gathered presents the city as a protected place of provision, a close parallel to the section’s fed and secured city.
terra: Qarun attributes his wealth to his own knowledge, while the verse recalls people stronger and greater in accumulation whom God destroyed; 28:81 exposes his inability to defend himself.

terra: Qarun goes out before his people in his adornment and attracts the desire of those who prefer worldly life, adding public display and the nearer life to the wealth that sinks into earth in 28:81.
terra: Qarun and his house are swallowed by the earth, and neither his company nor he can defend him, joining displayed wealth, downward engulfment, and discovered powerlessness.
luna: The secure sanctuary stands amid people seized around it; this supplies another specific city-and-safety formulation beside the section's city fed and made secure.
terra: The prosperous claim that their greater wealth and children mean they will not be punished, another explicit form of the section’s delusion that amassed property guarantees immunity.
terra: Shackles are placed around necks up to the chins, forcing heads upward; 36:9 then surrounds the people with barriers and covers them so that they cannot see.
terra: Barriers before and behind enclose the neck-shackled people of 36:8, and their sight is covered, joining closure with the failure of the eyes they were given.
luna: Mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify, turning the section's fear of being unseen into bodily evidence at judgment.
terra: فَاهْدُوهُمْ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطِ الْجَحِيمِ commands that wrongdoers be “guided” to the road of Hell, the sharpest reversal of a waymark that should lead the traveler safely.

luna: The section quotes the crowd “مُّقْتَحِمٌۭ” rushing in with the condemned; it is the image of plunging into fire opposite the unentered uphill passage. | terra: The arriving crowd is مُقْتَحِمٌ and will enter the Fire; its plunge into punishment reverses the unattempted اقتحام of the life-giving pass.

terra: When the disbelievers reach Hell its gates are opened and the keepers ask about the rejected signs; this opened-gate arrival forms a specific boundary with the section’s fire closed over those who denied the signs.
luna: The section places eyes beside the claim of being unseen; this ayah says God knows “خَآئِنَةَ ٱلْأَعْيُنِ” and what hearts conceal, closing that imagined privacy.
terra: With yokes around their necks and chains, the condemned are dragged onward; 40:72 supplies their movement into boiling water and fire, uniting the unopened neck and fiery destination.
terra: The neck-bound people of 40:71 are dragged through boiling water and then burned in the Fire, carrying the bond-to-fire movement in consecutive ayat.

luna: Hearing, sight, and skins testify against their owners, a specific answer to the section's person who thinks no one sees him. | terra: At the Fire, hearing, eyes, and skins testify against their owners, overturning the presumption that one’s acts went unseen; 41:21 explains that God made these witnesses speak.
terra: After bonds are secured in battle, captives may be released by favor or ransom; the scene gives a nonlexical instance of undoing a human bond, though it is not expressed as freeing a neck.

luna: Severing kinship ties is condemned, a specific reversal of the section's community that pities one another as though from one womb. | terra: أَن تُقَطِّعُوا أَرْحَامَكُمْ makes severing womb-ties the social reversal of acting as though others emerged from the same womb and extending mercy to them.

luna: The section's people who adhere like plants meet the crop here: it puts forth shoots, strengthens them, and grows firm, an image of connected growth. | terra: The believers are رُحَمَاءُ بَيْنَهُمْ and are likened to a crop whose shoots support and thicken one another, directly joining mutual mercy to the section’s image of people growing together like plants.

luna: Believers are called siblings and told to reconcile; this gives the section's people who pity one another as if from one womb a concrete communal counterpart. | terra: Believers are declared brothers and told to reconcile so that they may receive mercy, supporting the section’s movement from shared origin to mutual mercy without using the womb image itself.
luna: The section's bound-neck and unseen person meet the statement that God is nearer than “حَبْلِ ٱلْوَرِيدِ”; the hidden self is known even at the neck's life-line.
luna: Everything is created according to measure, a repeated formulation for the section's measurement motif and the human claim about power.

luna: The companions of the right name the same right-side company as 90:18, giving the section's right-hand outcome a repeated Quranic formulation. | terra: أَصْحَابُ الْمَيْمَنَةِ names the right-side company in a threefold division; 56:9 and 56:41 supply its left-side counterpart.

luna: The companions of the left provide the matching left-side boundary to the section's contrast between the two companies. | terra: أَصْحَابُ الْمَشْأَمَةِ gives the left-side company opposite 56:8, repeating the two-sided classification that frames the section’s end.
luna: This next description develops the companions of the right as a distinct saved group, completing the side label in 56:8.

luna: This next description develops the companions of the left amid heat and smoke, linking the side label in 56:9 with the section's fire-bound end. | terra: The companions of the left are named again as their punishment begins; 56:42 supplies the scorching air and boiling water of that adverse destination.
terra: فِي سَمُومٍ وَحَمِيمٍ gives the left-side company a burning environment, linking the adverse side to fiery punishment though it is not the section’s closed fire.
terra: God makes fire a تَذْكِرَةً and a benefit for travelers or desert users, supporting the section’s older wayfinding-and-provision sense of fire rather than its sealed punitive sense.
terra: A wall with a gate divides the two companies: mercy is inside and punishment outside, giving the section a concrete boundary between mutual mercy and the adverse fiery side.

terra: Competition in wealth and children is likened to rain-grown vegetation that pleases, dries, and becomes debris, making amassed worldly wealth a passing plant image rather than the section’s mutually supporting growth.

luna: In the separate zihar-expiration setting, return requires freeing a neck before the spouses touch; this repeats the section's release-of-a-neck act. | terra: The expiation for ẓihār requires تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ before the couple touch, another concrete act of opening bondage in a different expiatory setting.
luna: The next ayah requires feeding sixty poor people when that release is impossible, connecting release and feeding in a different expiation sequence.

terra: The distribution of public wealth includes relatives, orphans, needy people, and the traveler so that wealth does not circulate only among the rich, directly explaining the social redistribution enacted by the pass.

luna: The helpers prefer others over themselves even when in need and are protected from miserliness, giving a specific communal counterpart to the section's feeding and mutual mercy. | terra: The city’s residents prefer migrants over themselves وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ, showing the section’s communal mercy as giving under one’s own scarcity.
luna: The enemy group seems gathered, yet its hearts are divided; this reverses the section's plants adhering and community made tender by shared kinship.
terra: God has prescribed تَحِلَّةَ أَيْمَانِكُمْ, explicitly giving an oath a lawful dissolution and thus supporting the section’s movement from a tied oath to release.
terra: The one walking fallen on his face is set against the one walking upright on a straight path, a precise bodily contrast between earthbound movement and guided upright travel.

luna: The garden owners swear to harvest early; the section sets their oath against the city oath that opens toward feeding its poor. | terra: The garden owners أَقْسَمُوا to harvest at morning, beginning the oath that will be used to exclude the poor rather than open toward them.

luna: Their oath excludes even an exception (“وَلَا يَسْتَثْنُونَ”), making the binding of an oath serve the reverse purpose from the section's release and feeding. | terra: وَلَا يَسْتَثْنُونَ shows the owners making no exception as they bind themselves to the harvest plan; 68:24 states its exclusion of the poor.

luna: The owners' whispered rule, “لَا يَدْخُلَنَّهَا ... مِسْكِينٌ,” directly reverses the section's feeding of the hungry and poor. | terra: أَن لَّا يَدْخُلَنَّهَا الْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكُم مِّسْكِينٌ states the oath’s intended result: no poor person is to enter the garden, reversing an oath that opens into feeding.
terra: They set out عَلَىٰ حَرْدٍ قَادِرِينَ, imagining themselves capable of enforcing deprivation; 68:27 exposes their own loss, echoing the section’s failed claim to power.
terra: بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ makes the garden owners themselves deprived after they swore to deprive the poor person in 68:17 and 68:24.
terra: Receiving the book بِیَمِینِهِ supplies the successful right-hand counterpart to the left-hand figure whose punishment and neglected poor person the section follows.

luna: The section's left-side figure is the man given his record in his left hand, “بِشِمَالِهِۦ”; this starts the same judgment scene that binds his neck and exposes his neglect of the poor. | terra: The book is placed in the man’s left hand—بِشِمَالِهِ—establishing the left-side figure whose wealth, neck, and refusal to feed the poor the section brings together.

luna: The section's speaker who says he spent much wealth meets this man's confession that his wealth did not avail him, “مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّى مَالِيَهْ.” | terra: مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ makes the man confess that his wealth did not avail him, the direct outcome of trusting a piled and expended fortune.

luna: The section explicitly connects its “I spent” with “my power has perished”; the ayah's “هَلَكَ عَنِّى سُلْطَٰنِيَهْ” states the loss of the power he presumed. | terra: هَلَكَ عَنِّي سُلْطَانِيَهْ is the condemned man’s discovery that his power has vanished, answering the section’s boast of expended wealth and imagined invulnerability.

luna: The left-handed figure's punishment proceeds to restraint: “خُذُوهُ فَغُلُّوهُ” seizes and fetters the same man whose neck the section says is bound. | terra: خُذُوهُ فَغُلُّوهُ orders that the left-hand man be seized and shackled, turning the neck that was not freed into the site of restraint.

luna: This next step in the same judgment scene orders him into the Fire, completing the section's movement from bound neck to sealed fire. | terra: ثُمَّ الْجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ places the shackled man in the blaze between the neck-bond of 69:30 and the chain of 69:32.

luna: The chain extending seventy cubits gives a concrete binding of the neck that the section places beside release of a neck. | terra: The man is inserted into a seventy-cubit chain; together with the shackle in 69:30, this supplies the bound body opposite the section’s act of opening a neck.

luna: The neighboring ayah names the man's disbelief in God as part of the same sequence, linking the left-side outcome to the section's sign-deniers. | terra: The chained man did not believe in God the Magnificent; with 69:34, unbelief and refusing to urge food become the paired reasons for his left-side punishment.

luna: The section links the bound man with his failure to urge food for the poor; this ayah supplies that precise failure, “وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ.” | terra: Failure to urge طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ is given as a cause of the chained left-hand recipient’s punishment, gathering the needy person, withheld food, and the doomed side in one scene.
luna: The next account gives him no food except “غِسْلِينٍۢ”; after the section's cited failure to feed the poor, this is the specific food of the condemned man.
luna: The neighbor identifies that foul food as reserved for wrongdoers, completing the reversal between withholding food from the poor and one's own final ration.
luna: The announced blazing Fire is an explicit counterpart to the section's sealed Fire at the end of the refused way.
luna: The Fire calls those who turned away, a concrete joining of refusal and fiery destination like the section's unentered passage and covered signs.
luna: The same passage identifies the one who gathered wealth and hoarded it, joining refusal of the way to the wealth that the section says cannot save.
luna: The human is described as created anxious, a close formulation of the section's human created amid hardship and its uphill trial.
luna: When hardship touches him, he is impatient, specifying the panic against which the section says sabr on the ascent must hold.
luna: When good reaches him, he withholds it; this concretely reverses the section's feeding of the hungry and release of the bound.
luna: The righteous keep a known share in their wealth, making the section's act of spending for the needy a standing right rather than display.
luna: The next ayah names the share's recipients as the asker and deprived, directly meeting the section's poor and hungry mouth.
luna: Belief in the Day of Recompense supplies the judgmental setting for the wealth-share just named, like the section's right and left outcomes.
luna: Those who fear their Lord's punishment give a specific stance that accords with the section's patience and mercy before its fire boundary.
luna: The declaration that no one is secure from punishment reverses the section's arrogant assumption that no one can overpower him.
terra: Whoever turns away from the Lord’s reminder is made to enter an arduous, climbing punishment, turning ascent into penalty rather than the saving passage.
luna: The section's source word lubad for amassed wealth shares root l-b-d with “لِبَدًا,” a tightly packed crowd around the servant; the pile-image shifts from property to people pressing close.
terra: God says He extended ample wealth to the man who then opposed the signs and was burdened with ascent, bringing wealth into the punitive-climb scene of 74:16–17.
terra: إِنَّهُ كَانَ لِآيَاتِنَا عَنِيدًا gives denial of the signs as the reason for the punitive ascent in 74:17, matching the section’s rejected signs and fiery end.
terra: سَأُرْهِقُهُ صَعُودًا makes an arduous ascent a punishment for the wealthy man who resists the signs, reversing the saving ascent of the pass.
terra: إِلَّا أَصْحَابَ الْيَمِينِ identifies the right-side group who question the guilty; 74:44 supplies the guilty people’s failure to feed the needy.
terra: مَا سَلَكَكُمْ فِي سَقَرَ asks what inserted the guilty into Saqar, and their answer in 74:44 names failure to feed the needy; the row supplies the entry-into-fire hinge.
terra: The people of Saqar confess لَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ; 74:39 places the people of the right nearby and 74:42 asks what led the guilty into the fire.
luna: This creation scene says the human is tested and given hearing and sight, setting up the section's created person endowed with eyes and directed toward a moral choice.

luna: “هَدَيْنَٰهُ ٱلسَّبِيلَ” states that the path is shown and the human may be grateful or ungrateful, a direct parallel to the two ways in the section. | terra: God guides the human being to the way, after which he may be grateful or ungrateful, a direct moral branching of the shown road into two human responses.

luna: The same sequence moves from guidance to chains, shackles, and blazing fire for deniers, joining the section's shown path to the closed-fire boundary. | terra: Chains, iron collars, and a blaze are prepared for disbelievers; later in the same passage 76:8 depicts the righteous feeding a needy person, orphan, and captive, sharpening the bond-and-fire alternative to merciful feeding.

luna: The righteous give food to the needy, orphan, and captive together; this closely stages the section's hungry mouth, orphan, poor person, and released neck. | terra: They feed food despite loving it to مِسْكِينًا وَيَتِيمًا وَأَسِيرًا, placing the needy person, orphan, and bound captive together in the positive act required by the pass.
luna: The feeders say they act only for God's face and seek no thanks; that motive contrasts with the section's gift made for people to see.
luna: The preceding ayah asks what the human was created from, opening the same human creation-to-measure-to-path sequence.
luna: The human is created and “فَقَدَّرَهُۥ” (measured/shaped); this is a close formulation of the section's sequence from creation through measure.
luna: The next step after human creation and measure says “ٱلسَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُۥ,” the path was made easy, completing a creation-to-way sequence.

luna: The human is described as laboring arduously toward the Lord until meeting Him, giving the section's created hardship a path and destination. | terra: Humanity is addressed as toiling كَدْحًا toward its Lord and meeting Him; 84:7–12 divide that arduous journey into a right-hand reception and a fiery contrary end.

luna: The person given his record in the right hand receives an easy account, a judgment counterpart to the section's right-side company. | terra: The book given بِیَمِینِهِ begins the easy reckoning branch of the same toil, directly paralleling the section’s people of the right.

luna: The person given his record from behind his back meets the section's left-side boundary in a contrasting judgment image. | terra: The contrary recipient takes his book behind his back, a variant of the left-hand judgment scene that leads to the blaze in 84:12.

luna: The next ayah says that he will enter a blazing fire, completing the fire consequence of the preceding back-handed record. | terra: وَيَصْلَىٰ سَعِيرًا completes the adverse side of the human journey begun in 84:6 and set against the right-hand recipient in 84:7.

luna: The preceding ayah says God created and formed; with 87:3 it supplies the creation step in the section's create-measure-guide sequence. | terra: الَّذِي خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ supplies creation and fitting immediately before measuring and guidance in 87:3, completing the sequence the section sets beside the road.

luna: The section says Quran joins measuring and guidance in its order; “قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ” states that exact measure-then-guidance sequence. | terra: وَالَّذِي قَدَّرَ فَهَدَى places measuring and guidance in one sequence; 87:2 supplies the preceding creation and fitting that complete the order recalled in the section.
luna: The abundant provision makes a person claim honor, opening the same sequence that corrects him for failing to honor the orphan.
luna: When provision is restricted the person claims humiliation; this clarifies the section's hunger and counters treating material measure as a person's worth.

luna: This passage asks why the orphan is not honored, the reverse of the section's call to meet the passage by caring for a related orphan. | terra: لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ exposes failure toward the orphan as the correction to a wealth-based account of honor and humiliation.

luna: “وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ” directly repeats the failure to urge feeding the poor that the section joins to the bound man's fate. | terra: وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ joins the unfed needy person to the neglected orphan in 89:17 and the devoured wealth in 89:19–20.

luna: The same people consume inheritance greedily, a specific misuse of wealth against the orphan and kinship that the section calls into mercy. | terra: وَتَأْكُلُونَ التُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَّمًّا makes heaped consumption of inherited property the material setting for the adjacent neglect of orphan and poor.

luna: The section's amassed wealth and neglected hungry person meet the denunciation of loving wealth with excessive love, showing the inward attachment behind withholding. | terra: وَتُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا names excessive love of wealth immediately after the orphan, poor person, and amassed inheritance, closely matching the section’s clustered images.

luna: This passage opens a direct two-path parallel: the one who gives and is mindful follows the charitable ascent that the section sets against refusing the passage. | terra: فَأَمَّا مَنْ أَعْطَىٰ وَاتَّقَىٰ begins the giving branch of a paired road; 92:7 makes its destination ease, while 92:8–11 give the withholding branch.
luna: The giver's affirmation of the good completes the first path's stance, corresponding to the section's faith and mutual counsel alongside mercy.

luna: The giver is made at ease for ease; this explicitly casts moral choice as a way made passable, echoing the section's guided ways and difficult ascent. | terra: فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ promises ease to the giver, illuminating the section’s difficult ascent as a moral road that God makes traversable.

luna: The opposite person is miserly and thinks himself self-sufficient, directly meeting the section's wealthy man who assumes he cannot be overcome. | terra: The opposing traveler بَخِلَ وَاسْتَغْنَىٰ—hoards and imagines self-sufficiency—before being eased toward hardship and losing the benefit of wealth.
luna: The second path rejects the good, a specific counterpart to refusing the section's passage of release and feeding.

luna: The withholding person is made at ease for hardship, turning the section's unentered uphill path toward its opposite outcome. | terra: فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ is the withholding branch’s road to hardship, a reversal of both the pass’s saving difficulty and the giver’s ease in 92:7.

luna: The ayah says wealth will not avail its owner at the fall, a direct outcome for the self-assured spender whose wealth the section links to vanished power. | terra: وَمَا يُغْنِي عَنْهُ مَالُهُ إِذَا تَرَدَّىٰ joins useless wealth to a downward fall, reversing the section’s upward leap through giving.
luna: The declaration that guidance belongs to God meets the section's two guided ways and contrasts guidance with human claims of control.
luna: The warning of a blazing fire gives the rejected path the same fiery endpoint that the section contrasts with a fire used as a guide.
luna: This ayah specifies who enters that fire, helping define the boundary between the two sides of the section's image.
luna: The fire-bound person is described as denying and turning away, a compact parallel to the section's deniers of signs who refuse the passage.
luna: The other path is kept away from the fire, giving the section's right-side people a clear counterpart to its fire-enclosed side.
luna: The God-conscious person gives wealth to purify himself, directly joining the section's spending, care for the poor, and upward moral movement.
luna: The gift is not repayment for a favor owed, clarifying a motive opposite the section's display for people to see.
luna: The giver seeks the face of the Most High Lord, specifying the inward audience that replaces the section's ostentatious giving for people.
luna: The closing assurance of satisfaction completes this giving path's outcome, beside the section's right-side destination.

luna: The speaker recalls finding the addressee an orphan and sheltering him, a direct orphan-and-protection scene for the section's kinless child. | terra: God found the addressee an orphan and gave shelter, beginning a remembered passage in which prior need becomes the reason not to oppress the orphan or repel the petitioner.

luna: The same address recalls finding the addressee needy and enriching him, meeting the section's transition from hunger to provision. | terra: God found the addressee in need and enriched him; 93:9–10 turn that remembered provision into duties toward the orphan and the asker.
terra: فَأَمَّا الْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ commands that the orphan not be oppressed, converting the shelter remembered in 93:6 into care for another orphan.

luna: The command not to repel the asker carries the same concrete compassion as the section's feeding of one in need. | terra: وَأَمَّا السَّائِلَ فَلَا تَنْهَرْ pairs the petitioner with the orphan of 93:9 and makes received provision answer another needy mouth.
luna: The promise that ease accompanies hardship speaks directly to the section's human created amid toil and its difficult ascent.
luna: This repeated promise confirms that the arduous passage is accompanied by ease, not a closed end.

luna: The oath by the secure city repeats the section's opening oath on the city, adding security as the city's stated quality. | terra: وَهَذَا الْبَلَدِ الْأَمِينِ is an oath by the secure city; 95:4–5 then move from human creation at the best stature to the lowest state, closely repeating the section’s city-oath and vertical human movement.

luna: The next ayah says the human was created in the best form, adding a human-creation formulation to the section's created person and faculties. | terra: Humanity is created in the best stature immediately after the oath by the secure city, supplying the elevated starting possibility that 95:5 then reverses.

luna: The human can be brought to the lowest low, a direct vertical reversal of the section's ascent and its person who clings to earth. | terra: ثُمَّ رَدَدْنَاهُ أَسْفَلَ سَافِلِينَ sends the human being to the lowest of the low, a direct vertical reversal of rising through the pass.
luna: Believers who do good deeds are excepted and receive an unfailing reward, specifying how the descent is reversed by the section's charitable way.
luna: The section's self-assured man thinks no one can master him; this passage says the human transgresses when he sees himself self-sufficient, naming the same false independence.
luna: This adjoining ayah identifies the conceit—“أَن رَّءَاهُ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ”—that makes the section's imagined immunity from power and sight possible.

luna: Against the section's person who thinks no one sees him, this warning asks whether he knows that God sees, “بِأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَرَىٰ.” | terra: أَلَمْ يَعْلَم بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ يَرَى answers the section’s human presumption that no one sees him, especially when he spends to be seen by people.
luna: Anyone who has done an atom's weight of good will see it, directly countering the section's assumption that no one sees and making small deeds visible.
luna: The same rule makes even an atom's weight of evil visible, giving the section's unseen person an exact boundary at judgment.
luna: Deeds are weighed, connecting the section's measure/capacity language to the judgment that sorts people by what they have done.
luna: The next ayah gives the heavy-scale person a pleasing life, completing one measured outcome beside the section's right-side company.
luna: The light-scale person supplies the opposite result to the section's right-side path.
luna: The next ayah names the light-scale person's destination as the abyss, completing the adverse measured outcome.
luna: This ayah asks what the abyss is, continuing the measured-judgment scene.
luna: The abyss is specified as a blazing fire, joining measured deeds to the section's fire-bound side.

luna: This closing ayah explicitly joins faith and good works with mutual counsel to truth and patience, repeating one of the section's named acts and its collective form. | terra: The saved people تَوَاصَوْا بِالصَّبْرِ, repeating the section’s distinctive act of mutually exhorting patience as a communal practice rather than solitary endurance toward fire.

luna: The section's word lubad for amassed wealth meets this ayah's collecting and counting of wealth; it makes the piled-up property a sign of false security. | terra: الَّذِي جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ portrays accumulated, repeatedly counted wealth in the same passage that ends with fire closed over its people in 104:8.

luna: The wealth-collector imagines his wealth will make him immortal, sharpening the section's portrait of a man who assumes no one can overpower him. | terra: يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُ أَخْلَدَهُ states the wealth-holder’s delusion of immunity, corresponding to the section’s man who imagines no one can master or even see him.
luna: The gatherer of wealth is cast into the Crusher, beginning a punishment sequence that ends in the shut Fire linked by the section to its closing image.
luna: This ayah asks what the Crusher is, extending the same wealth-and-fire warning toward its explicit fire description.
luna: The Crusher is described as God's kindled fire, a neighboring specification of the fire shut over people in 104:8.
luna: The fire reaches the hearts, adding its inward effect to the closed-fire scene the section links with denied signs.

luna: The section identifies the root wāw-ṣād-dāl as closing; this ayah uses “مُّؤْصَدَةٌ” for the Fire shut over its people, a direct counterpart to 90:20. | terra: إِنَّهَا عَلَيْهِم مُّؤْصَدَةٌ repeats the image of fire closed over its people and therefore supplies the closest external instance of the surah’s final closure.

luna: The next ayah says the shut Fire is in extended columns, completing the enclosure that the section's closed-fire image evokes. | terra: فِي عَمَدٍ مُّمَدَّدَةٍ adds extended columns to the closure of 104:8, specifying how the fire remains shut over its people.

luna: The section joins city and hunger through the dictionary gloss “orphan in famine”; this ayah names the city-feeding counterpart, “أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍۢ,” and security from fear. | terra: God أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍ and secured them from fear, giving the section its direct Quranic scene of a city’s people fed through hunger.

luna: The denier of judgment “يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ” (repels the orphan), a direct reversal of the section's demanded care for the orphan. | terra: The denier is identified as the one who drives away الْيَتِيمَ, beginning a compact scene that joins the orphan to withheld food and show in worship.

luna: This ayah condemns failing to urge feeding the needy, matching the section's repeated link between an un-fed poor person and failed passage. | terra: He does not urge طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ; 107:2 supplies the rejected orphan and 107:6 the display before human eyes, reproducing several of the section’s meetings.

luna: The root r-y-ʾ appears here in “يُرَآءُونَ” for people who show off their prayer; it extends the section's public display from spending to worship. | terra: الَّذِينَ هُمْ يُرَاءُونَ adds ostentatious display to the same passage that rejects the orphan and refuses to urge feeding the needy.

luna: The showy worshipers then withhold even small aid, a pointed reversal of the section's visible performance versus feeding and mercy. | terra: The show-offs withhold even الْمَاعُونَ, making refusal of small material aid the last act in the orphan-and-hunger sequence of 107:2–6.
terra: مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُ وَمَا كَسَبَ denies that wealth and earnings avail, and 111:3 immediately gives the fiery destination.
terra: سَيَصْلَىٰ نَارًا ذَاتَ لَهَبٍ makes fire the end of the wealth that could not avail in 111:2, condensing the section’s movement from piled property to fire.
